title: Discourse markers in spoken English
subtitle: well, anyway, mind you, hang on
summary: Use the little words that organise conversation - well, anyway, mind you, listen, still and I mean - so that your spoken English sounds natural.

lesson.heading: What are discourse markers?
lesson.text: Discourse markers are expressions which organise, comment on or frame what we are saying. They do not add new information; they tell the listener what you are doing with the information.

examples.text: *A:* So you live in Boston? *B:* **Well**, near Boston.
examples.note: well shows the speaker is not giving the expected yes answer

examples.text: **Right**, let's have a look at exercise 3.
examples.note: right and OK organise what happens next, e.g. in a classroom

lesson.heading: Organising a conversation
lesson.text: These markers move a conversation from one stage to the next. **Now then** is used by someone in control, such as a teacher. **Fine** and **Great** often close a conversation.

examples.text: **So**, would you like to come to the table now, please?
**Good**, I'll ring you on Thursday, then.
**Fine**, let's meet again next week, then, shall we?
**So, where was I?** I was telling you about my aunt ...
examples.note: used after an interruption, to come back to the main story

lesson.heading: Modifying and commenting on what you say
rows: It's cold, isn't it? Mind you, it's November.
introduces a suggestion or an important point
Listen, why don't you let me sort it out?
What's her number? Let me see, I have it here somewhere ...
Hang on! Let me tell you what he said!
I can't do that. You see, I'm not the boss here.
We shouldn't be too hard on him. I mean, he's only a child.

lesson.heading: Hesitating and being vague
lesson.text: When you are not sure of the best way to say something, English speakers use **sort of**, **kind of**, **like** and **you know**. They give you thinking time and make what you say less definite.

examples.text: He was, **you know**, **sort of** ... just standing there.
He was wearing this, **kind of**, cowboy hat.
We were just sitting in the garden, **sort of** doing nothing much.

left.label: anyway - the topic can now change
left.text: The speaker thinks the subject is finished, or that the conversation can close.
examples: So that's what we have to do. **Anyway**, I'll ring you tomorrow.
Yes, there is a lot of work to do. **Anyway**, I must rush now, I'll call you tomorrow.

right.label: still / on the other hand - two ideas contrasted
right.text: The speaker sets one idea against another.
examples: It rained all day yesterday. **Still**, we can't complain, it was fine all last week.
He loses his temper very quickly. **On the other hand**, he's got a great sense of humour.

lesson.heading: Listing points out loud
lesson.text: In informal spoken English, people use the letters of the alphabet - usually no more than **a**, **b** and **c** - to list the points they want to make.

examples.text: *Stella:* Why aren't you going this evening? *Adam:* Well, **a)** I haven't got any money, and **b)** it's too far anyway.
There are two reasons why I think he's wrong: **a**, people don't act like that, and **b**, Paul would certainly never act like that.

lesson.text: Choose three or four markers you like and use them - but do not overuse them, or your speech will sound padded rather than natural.

exercises.prompt: Match each discourse marker with its function.

pairs.right: gains time while you remember something
signals that the topic can change

exercises.prompt: *A:* Are you a football fan? *B:* ___, I like it but I wouldn't say I was a fan.
exercises.explanation: Well warns the listener that the answer is not the expected one.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Which number is yours? *B:* ___ ... it's that one there, yes, that one.
exercises.explanation: Let me see gains a little time while the speaker looks or thinks.

exercises.prompt: *A:* I saw this funny old man and I stopped him ... *B:* I bet it was Jim Dibble! *A:* ___! Let me tell you what happened first.
exercises.explanation: Hang on and hold on prevent an interruption.

exercises.prompt: *A:* What are we going to do? *B:* ___, I've got an idea. Why don't we ask James to help?
exercises.explanation: Listen and look introduce a suggestion or an important point.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Money isn't the most important thing in life. *B:* ___, you can't live without it!
exercises.explanation: Still contrasts the second idea with the first, like on the other hand.

exercises.prompt: *A:* He's looking exhausted. *B:* Really? *A:* ___, look at his eyes - he looks so tired.
exercises.explanation: I mean introduces an explanation of what you have just said.

exercises.prompt: *A:* So I'll pick you up at 6.30. *B:* ___ See you then.
exercises.explanation: Great, fine and good are typical markers for closing a conversation.

exercises.prompt: Which marker would a teacher use to get a class's attention: '___, I want you to pay attention, everyone.'
exercises.explanation: Now and now then are used by the person in control of the conversation.

exercises.prompt: 'You seem a bit sad today. ___, let me buy lunch for you to cheer you up.' Which marker fits?
Sort these markers by what they mainly do.

exercises.statement: In 'It's cold, isn't it? Mind you, it's November,' the marker *mind you* works rather like *however*.
exercises.explanation: Correct - mind you introduces an afterthought that qualifies what was just said.

exercises.statement: *So, where was I?* is used to change to a completely new subject.
exercises.explanation: It is used after an interruption to come back to the main topic or story.

exercises.prompt: Put this speaker's words in order.
exercises.answer: We shouldn't be too hard on him. I mean, he's only a child.
exercises.explanation: I mean introduces the reason that makes the first statement clear.
